hook.text: Banks earn $100 billion annually from interchange fees. Most people don't know they exist.

buildup.text: When a merchant accepts your Visa card, their bank pays your bank a fee—usually 1.5-2%.

discovery.text: Credit card rewards—cashback, points, miles—are funded by these interchange fees from merchants.

twist.text: Merchants pass the cost to all customers via higher prices. Even cash payers subsidize card rewards.

climax.text: The EU capped interchange at 0.3%. US fees remain 5x higher, funding richer reward programs.

punchline.text: Your cashback rewards are paid by every customer's higher prices.

quiz.question: Who ultimately pays for credit card reward programs?

details.summary: Interchange fees are payments from the merchant's bank to the cardholder's bank on every card transaction, typically 1.5 to 2% of the purchase amount. These fees fund card rewards programs and are the economic foundation of the credit card industry's business model.
details.whyItMatters: Interchange fees represent the hidden cost embedded in every card purchase, ultimately paid by consumers through higher prices. They fund the rewards programs that drive card usage while creating billions in revenue for issuing banks.
takeaways: Merchant banks pay cardholder banks a fee on every card transaction
Interchange fees fund rewards programs, fraud protection, and bank profits
Higher interchange in the US funds richer rewards than in regions with caps

faq.question: Why are interchange fees controversial among merchants?
faq.answer: Merchants pay billions in interchange fees annually and cannot negotiate rates set by Visa and Mastercard. These fees effectively increase the cost of goods by 2-3%. Small merchants are disproportionately affected because they lack volume to negotiate better rates from processors.

faq.question: How do interchange fees differ across countries?
faq.answer: US interchange averages around 2% while the EU caps interchange at 0.3% for credit cards. Australia, Canada, and India also regulate rates. Lower interchange means less generous rewards programs. American Express charges even higher fees, which is why some merchants refuse it.
